extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientists and graduate students interested in the nature of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how scientific paradigms shape perception, data, measurement, and experimentation, and how paradigm shifts (scientific revolutions) change what scientists see and do. Discusses normal science, anomalies, crises, gestalt switches, and the paradigm-dependence of operations and classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm-induced changes of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: After a paradigm change scientists may literally 'see' different phenomena in the same objects (e.g., Copernicans seeing different heavens, Lavoisier seeing oxygen where Priestley saw dephlogisticated air, Galileo seeing a pendulum rather than constrained fall).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: astronomy (comets, planets), electricity (repulsion vs attraction before/after Hauksbee and Franklin), chemistry (oxygen vs dephlogisticated air), Galileo's pendulum. Kuhn emphasizes that these are not merely reinterpretations but changes in perceptual experience brought about by the paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science as articulation and refinement of a paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science aims to 'refine, extend, and articulate a paradigm that is already in existence' and depends on the paradigm to define what counts as a datum, what instruments to use, and what concepts are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of observations is central within normal science because the paradigm already defines measurement targets and conceptual categories; examples include Galileo interpreting pendulum-related measurements to yield laws accessible within his paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradox: paradigms are not corrigible by normal science
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science cannot correct a paradigm; it can only reveal anomalies that lead to crisis, which is then terminated by a relatively sudden and unstructured event like a gestalt switch (scientific revolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn claims paradigms resist piecemeal correction; discovery of anomalies leads to crisis and then to intuition-like 'flashes' or gestalt switches (e.g., the scales falling from the eyes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and observations are not unequivocally stable
rubrics_metrics.description: The data that scientists collect are themselves different under different paradigms; a pendulum is not the same datum as a falling stone, and oxygen is not the same datum as dephlogisticated air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because what counts as evidence is paradigm-determined, purportedly 'raw' observations cannot be assumed fixed across paradigms; Kuhn uses historical examples to show measurements and observable regularities differ with paradigms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory operations and measurements are paradigm-determined
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations and measurements are 'not the given' but 'the collected with difficulty'—they are concrete indices to perceptions and are selected because they promise fruitful elaboration of the accepted paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different paradigms make different laboratory manipulations relevant (e.g., measurements relevant to a pendulum differ from those relevant to constrained fall); thus experimental design and which measurements are pursued depend on paradigm commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempts at a neutral observation-language presuppose paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts to construct a language of pure percepts or neutral observation-language inevitably presuppose a paradigm and embody expectations about nature, so they cannot deliver purely objective, context-free data reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn cites psychological evidence (duck-rabbit, inverting lenses) and Goodman to argue that observation-languages are constrained by prior theoretical or everyday paradigms and fail when those expectations are violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms determine large integrated areas of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigm changes simultaneously reshape perception and conceptualization across many related phenomena (e.g., adopting oxygen changes views of compounds, ores, and many substances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing a central term or classification (like 'planet' or 'condensor'/'Leyden jar') affects a network of related concepts and observations; paradigms determine broad experiential categories, not single isolated items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same operation can index different natural regularities under different paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: A laboratory operation that had one meaning under the old paradigm can become an index to a different aspect of nature when attached to a new paradigm (Dalton/affinity vs atomic theory examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn uses eighteenth-century chemistry: operations used to justify viewing solutions as compounds under affinity theory were reinterpreted once Dalton's atomic theory created a new framework and anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some manipulations become irrelevant after revolution but many endure with changed role
rubrics_metrics.description: Postrevolutionary science includes many of the same manipulations, instruments, and terms as prerevolutionary science, but their relation to the paradigm and possibly their concrete results change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn emphasizes continuity in instruments and language, while also noting that the significance and interpretation of those operations are altered by the new paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual training and community/culture embed paradigms in experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists (and laymen) do not learn perception piecemeal; conceptual and manipulative categories are learned together, so community and cultural training help constitute what scientists 'see'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies: a child's learning 'mama' simultaneously changes many expectations; similarly, adoption of Copernican or other paradigms reshapes a scientist's perceptual world across many phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestalt/intuitive nature of paradigm shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: The birth of a new paradigm often involves intuition or gestalt-like transformations (flashes, dreams) that are not reducible to stepwise interpretation of existing data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn notes Hadamard's accounts of intuition in discovery and argues these flashes gather up large portions of experience and transform them wholesale rather than by piecemeal logical inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational/definitional questions presuppose paradigm recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about what measurements or retinal imprints make X what it is presuppose that the questioner can already recognize X under a given paradigm; such operational queries are part of normal science and depend on prior paradigmatic subdivision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: asking what makes a pendulum a pendulum presupposes one already recognizes the pendulum; if one sees constrained fall instead, the question cannot even be posed in the same terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification (e.g., mixture vs compound) depends on paradigm, not only definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctions like mixture vs compound were determined by eighteenth-century affinity theory and are not merely verbal: operational criteria and interpretive frameworks supported treating solutions as compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn argues operational tests did not fully separate mixtures from compounds; the paradigm (affinity theory) shaped both classification and the experimental expectations that upheld it until Dalton's atomic theory created anomalies.
